claims.text: High strength and strength retention in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV RHEAs are attributable to edge dislocations.
The thermoelastic behavior of RHEAs is governed by the mobility and density of edge dislocations.
Trace interstitial impurity concentration strongly influences edge-dislocation density and mobility.
Low impurity levels maintain a stable network of mobile edge dislocations that supports high strength.
Oxygen and nitrogen interstitials initially provide solid-solution strengthening in a Ti-V-Nb-Ta RHEA.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during aging at 700°C in a Ti-V-Nb-Ta RHEA.
Aging-induced phase segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the metal matrix.
Depletion of matrix interstitials reduces dislocation pinning and makes edge-dislocation glide easier.
Interstitial depletion during aging produces progressive mechanical softening with aging time.
Increasing oxygen or nitrogen concentration will cause more phase segregation than occurs in a low-impurity control subjected to the same aging treatment.
Higher-impurity RHEAs will have lower yield strength than low-impurity controls after high-temperature aging.
Higher-impurity aged samples will contain fewer effective dislocation-pinning points.
Higher interstitial content and aging will alter thermal expansion behavior relative to the baseline.
Low-impurity, minimally aged RHEAs have stable thermoelastic properties because edge dislocations dominate their deformation.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase RHEAs between approximately 700°C and 1000°C under inert conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially multiphase RHEAs or to RHEAs in oxidizing environments.

contradictions.description: The narrative baseline is minimally aged, whereas the falsification experiment correctly gives both impurity groups identical aging treatments. Comparing an aged high-impurity sample with a minimally aged baseline would confound impurity concentration with aging duration.

The design deliberately varies impurity level, but the falsification rule says 'after controlling for impurity levels.' Read literally, controlling impurity level would remove the intervention being tested; the intended criterion is presumably after controlling all variables other than impurity level.
